                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## Validations and Preparations\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Generic actions support validations and preparations, allowing you to add business logic and input validation to your actions.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'### Validations\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Validations in generic actions work similarly to those in other action types. They validate the action input before the action logic runs.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'action :create_user, :struct do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  constraints instance_of: __MODULE__\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :name, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :email, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :age, :integer\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  validate present([:name, :email])\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  validate match(:email, ~r/@/)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  validate compare(:age, greater_than: 13) do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    message "Must be at least 13 years old"\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    # Create user logic here\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    {:ok, %__MODULE__{\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      name: input.arguments.name,\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      email: input.arguments.email,\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      age: input.arguments.age\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    }}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'You can also use custom validation modules:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'action :transfer_funds, :boolean do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :from_account, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :to_account, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :amount, :decimal, allow_nil?: false'[39m,
                  isTruncated: [33mfalse[39m

                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m"There is a built in data layer that is useful for testing and prototyping, that uses [ETS](https://elixir-lang.org/getting-started/mix-otp/ets.html). ETS (Erlang Term Storage) is OTP's in-memory database, so the data won't actually stick around beyond the lifespan of your program, but it's a simple way to try things out.\n"[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'To add it to your resource, modify it like so:\n'[39m +

                    [32m'  domain: Helpdesk.Support,\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  data_layer: Ash.DataLayer.Ets\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Now we can slightly modify our code above, by removing the `Ash.DataLayer.Simple.set_data/2` calls, and we can see our persistence in action. Remember, ETS is in-memory, meaning restarting your application/iex session will remove all of the data.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m"# Use this to pick up changes you've made to your code, or restart your session\n"[39m +
                    [32m'recompile()\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'require Ash.Query\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'for i <- 0..5 do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  ticket =\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    Helpdesk.Support.Ticket\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    |> Ash.Changeset.for_create(:open, %{subject: "Issue #{i}"})\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    |> Ash.create!()\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  if rem(i, 2) == 0 do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    ticket\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    |> Ash.Changeset.for_update(:close)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    |> Ash.update!()\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'# Show the tickets where the subject contains "2"\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Helpdesk.Support.Ticket\n'[39m +
                    [32m'|> Ash.Query.filter(contains(subject, "2"))\n'[39m +
                    [32m'|> Ash.read!()\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +

                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Field policies allow you to authorize access to specific fields via policies scoped to fields.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +

                    [32m'If _any_ field policies exist then _all_ fields must be authorized by a field policy.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'If you want a "deny-list" style, then you can add policies for specific fields.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'and add a catch-all policy using the special field name `:*`. All policies that apply\n'[39m +
                    [32m'to a field must be authorized.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The only exception to the above behavior is primary keys, which can always be read by everyone.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Additionally, keep in mind that adding `Ash.Policy.Authorizer` will require that all actions\n'[39m +
                    [32m'pass policies. If you want to just add field policies, you will need to add a policy that allows\n'[39m +
                    [32m'all access explicitly, i.e\n'[39m +

                    [32m'### Using Expressions In Field Policies\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Unlike in regular policies, expressions in field policies cannot refer to related entities currently (except when using exists). Instead, you will need to create aggregates or expression calculations that return the results you want to reference.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'In results, forbidden fields will be replaced with a special value: `%Ash.ForbiddenField{}`.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'When these fields are referred to in filters, they will be replaced with an expression that evaluates to `nil`. To support this behavior, only simple and filter checks are allowed in field policies.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'### Handling private fields in internal functions\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'When calling internal functions like `Ash.read!/1`, private fields will by default always be shown.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Even if field policies apply to the resource. You can change the default behaviour by setting the\n'[39m +
                    [32m'`private_fields` option on field policies.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'field_policies do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  private_fields :include\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The different options are:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- `:show` will always show private fields\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- `:hide` will always hide private fields\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- `:include` will let you to write field policies for private fields and private fields\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  will be shown or hidden depending on the outcome of the policy\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'If you want to overwrite the default option that is `:show`, you can do that by setting a global flag:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +

                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## References to related data & fields\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'### Calculations\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The dependencies of a calculation do not have any authorization applied to them. This includes the dependencies loaded with `c:Ash.Resource.Calculation.load/3`, as well as any dependencies referenced in a calculation expression. To understand why this is the case, take the following calculation:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'calculate :users_ssn_last_4, :string, expr(fragment("RIGHT(?, 4)", user.ssn))\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The `user` record may not be visible to the actor loading this calculation, and if it is, the `ssn` field may not be visible due to field policies. If calculations authorized access to their dependencies, you would *never* be able to write a calculation like the above.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'#### Aggregates\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Aggregates are the one exception to the above. Aggregates referenced *anywhere* will *always* authorize access to the related data they reference (unless `authorize?: false` is set when running the action). They will not, however, authorize references to the\n'[39m +
                    [32m'actual field that they refer to. For example, you may not allow managers to see the email\n'[39m +
                    [32m'of their team members, but they are allowed to know something like "how many team members\n'[39m +
                    [32m'have set up their email". So in an aggregate like the following:\n'[39m +

                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'if the field policies were applied to `:email`, that number would always show `0`,\n'[39m +
                    [32m'because all `:email` attributes would appear to be `nil` to the manager.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'### Fields annotated as `input`\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m"When you use `Ash.Query.filter_input` or `Ash.Query.sort_input` (which extensions like `AshGraphql` and `AshJsonApi` do when filters/sorts are provided by the user), the contained field references are annotated as `input`. The following rules are honored for field references annotated as `input` only. Per the above section, the *contents* of a calculation's expression referenced in filters are never annotated as `input`, although the calculation itself will be, so that you can write field policies on calculations.\n"[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'#### Relationship paths in filters\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m"When a field is referenced at a relationship path, the authorization rules for that related resource's primary read action (or the relationship's configured `:read_action`) will be applied to the filter as well. For example, say that you have a `User` resource, and a `Post` resource. The `User` resource can only be read by the actor if their id matches the user's id (i.e they can only read themselves).\n"[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +

                [32m'\n'[39m +

                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'| role          | capabilities                                         |\n'[39m +

                [32m'| `:viewer`     | `read`                                               |\n'[39m +

                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'### Permission resolution (this precedence is normative)\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m"An actor's effective roles at an org unit `U` are resolved per role, independently, as follows.\n"[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'1. Build the path `U`, `parent(U)`, `parent(parent(U))`, …, up to the root — nearest unit first.\n'[39m +
                [32m'2. For role `R`, walk that path from nearest to root and stop at the **first** unit that carries at\n'[39m +
                [32m'   least one `RoleAssignment` for this actor with that role.\n'[39m +
                [32m'3. If no unit on the path carries such an assignment, the actor does not hold `R` at `U`.\n'[39m +
                [32m'4. If the stopping unit carries **any** assignment for this actor and role with `effect: :deny`,\n'[39m +
                [32m'   the actor does not hold `R` at `U` — even if an ancestor granted it, and even if the same unit\n'[39m +
                [32m'   also carries a `:grant` for it.\n'[39m +
                [32m'5. Otherwise the actor holds `R` at `U`.\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m"The actor's capabilities at `U` are the union of the capabilities of every role held at `U`. A grant\n"[39m +
                [32m'therefore flows down the whole subtree, a deny at a descendant cuts it off for that subtree, and a\n'[39m +
                [32m'grant deeper still re-establishes it.\n'[39m +

                    [32m'pass policies. If you want to just add field policies, you will need to add a policy that allows\n'[39m +
                    [32m'all access explicitly, i.e\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'policies do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  policy always() do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    authorize_if always()\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'### Using Expressions In Field Policies\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Unlike in regular policies, expressions in field policies cannot refer to related entities currently (except when using exists). Instead, you will need to create aggregates or expression calculations that return the results you want to reference.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'In results, forbidden fields will be replaced with a special value: `%Ash.ForbiddenField{}`.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'When these fields are referred to in filters, they will be replaced with an expression that evaluates to `nil`. To support this behavior, only simple and filter checks are allowed in field policies.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'### Handling private fields in internal functions\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'When calling internal functions like `Ash.read!/1`, private fields will by default always be shown.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Even if field policies apply to the resource. You can change the default behaviour by setting the\n'[39m +
                    [32m'`private_fields` option on field policies.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'field_policies do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  private_fields :include\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The different options are:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- `:show` will always show private fields\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- `:hide` will always hide private fields\n'[39m +
                    [32m'- `:include` will let you to write field policies for private fields and private fields\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  will be shown or hidden depending on the outcome of the policy\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'If you want to overwrite the default option that is `:show`, you can do that by setting a global flag:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'config :ash, :policies, private_fields: :include\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'## References to related data & fields\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'### Calculations\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The dependencies of a calculation do not have any authorization applied to them. This includes the dependencies loaded with `c:Ash.Resource.Calculation.load/3`, as well as any dependencies referenced in a calculation expression. To understand why this is the case, take the following calculation:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'calculate :users_ssn_last_4, :string, expr(fragment("RIGHT(?, 4)", user.ssn))\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'The `user` record may not be visible to the actor loading this calculation, and if it is, the `ssn` field may not be visible due to field policies. If calculations authorized access to their dependencies, you would *never* be able to write a calculation like the above.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'#### Aggregates\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Aggregates are the one exception to the above. Aggregates referenced *anywhere* will *always* authorize access to the related data they reference (unless `authorize?: false` is set when running the action). They will not, however, authorize references to the\n'[39m +
                    [32m'actual field that they refer to. For example, you may not allow managers to see the email\n'[39m +
                    [32m'of their team members, but they are allowed to know something like "how many team members\n'[39m +
                    [32m'have set up their email". So in an aggregate like the following:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'aggregate :users_with_email, :count, :email\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'if the field policies were applied to `:email`, that number would always show `0`,\n'[39m +
                    [32m'because all `:email` attributes would appear to be `nil` to the manager.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'### Fields annotated as `input`\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m"When you use `Ash.Query.filter_input` or `Ash.Query.sort_input` (which extensions like `AshGraphql` and `AshJsonApi` do when filters/sorts are provided by the user), the contained field references are annotated as `input`. The following rules are honored for field references annotated as `input` only. Per the above section, the *contents* of a calculation's expression referenced in filters are never annotated as `input`, although the calculation itself will be, so that you can write field policies on calculations.\n"[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'#### Relationship paths in filters\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m"When a field is referenced at a relationship path, the authorization rules for that related resource's primary read action (or the relationship's configured `:read_action`) will be applied to the filter as well. For example, say that you have a `User` resource, and a `Post` resource. The `User` resource can only be read by the actor if their id matches the user's id (i.e they can only read themselves).\n"[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +

                    [32m'policy action_type(:read) do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  authorize_if expr(id == ^actor(:id))\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Given a filter like `Ash.Query.filter_input(Post, %{user: %{email: "example@example.com"}})`, the resulting filter expression would be:\n'[39m +

                    [32m'    user.id == ^actor(:id)\n'[39m +
                    [32m')\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'This prevents a common security vulnerability that would allow malicious actors to "sniff" related data by providing filters over `User`, and seeing what `Post` records are returned.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'#### Field references in filters & sorts\n'[39m +

                    [32m'    user.email'[39m,

                [32m'### Permission resolution (this precedence is normative)\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +

                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'1. Build the path `U`, `parent(U)`, `parent(parent(U))`, …, up to the root — nearest unit first.\n'[39m +
                [32m'2. For role `R`, walk that path from nearest to root and stop at the **first** unit that carries at\n'[39m +
                [32m'   least one `RoleAssignment` for this actor with that role.\n'[39m +
                [32m'3. If no unit on the path carries such an assignment, the actor does not hold `R` at `U`.\n'[39m +
                [32m'4. If the stopping unit carries **any** assignment for this actor and role with `effect: :deny`,\n'[39m +

                [32m'5. Otherwise the actor holds `R` at `U`.\n'[39m +

                    [32m'  run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    {:ok, "Hello: #{input.arguments.name}"}\n'[39m +

                    [32m'## Validations and Preparations\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Generic actions support validations and preparations, allowing you to add business logic and input validation to your actions.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'### Validations\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Validations in generic actions work similarly to those in other action types. They validate the action input before the action logic runs.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'action :create_user, :struct do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  constraints instance_of: __MODULE__\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :name, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :email, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :age, :integer\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  validate present([:name, :email])\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  validate match(:email, ~r/@/)\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  validate compare(:age, greater_than: 13) do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    message "Must be at least 13 years old"\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    # Create user logic here\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    {:ok, %__MODULE__{\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      name: input.arguments.name,\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      email: input.arguments.email,\n'[39m +
                    [32m'      age: input.arguments.age\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    }}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'You can also use custom validation modules:\n'[39m +

                [32m'* `id` — uuid primary key\n'[39m +

                [32m'* `budget_cents` — `:integer`, required, default `0`\n'[39m +

                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'Each role confers exactly this set of capabilities:\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'| role          | capabilities                                         |\n'[39m +
                [32m'| ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |\n'[39m +
                [32m'| `:viewer`     | `read`                                               |\n'[39m +
                [32m'| `:editor`     | `read`, `write`                                      |\n'[39m +
                [32m'| `:auditor`    | `read`, `view_budget`                                |\n'[39m +
                [32m'| `:unit_admin` | `read`, `write`, `delete`, `relocate`, `view_budget` |\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'### Permission resolution (this precedence is normative)\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m"An actor's effective roles at an org unit `U` are resolved per role, independently, as follows.\n"[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m'1. Build the path `U`, `parent(U)`, `parent(parent(U))`, …, up to the root — nearest unit first.\n'[39m +
                [32m'2. For role `R`, walk that path from nearest to root and stop at the **first** unit that carries at\n'[39m +
                [32m'   least one `RoleAssignment` for this actor with that role.\n'[39m +
                [32m'3. If no unit on the path carries such an assignment, the actor does not hold `R` at `U`.\n'[39m +
                [32m'4. If the stopping unit carries **any** assignment for this actor and role with `effect: :deny`,\n'[39m +
                [32m'   the actor does not hold `R` at `U` — even if an ancestor granted it, and even if the same unit\n'[39m +
                [32m'   also carries a `:grant` for it.\n'[39m +
                [32m'5. Otherwise the actor holds `R` at `U`.\n'[39m +
                [32m'\n'[39m +
                [32m"The actor's capabilities at `U` are the union of the capabilities of every role held at `U`. A grant\n"[39m +
                [32m'therefore flows down the whole subtree, a deny at a descendant cuts it off for that subtree, and a\n'[39m +
                [32m'grant deeper still re-establishes it.\n'[39m +

                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'To execute a generic action in Ash, follow these steps:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'1. **Prepare the action input:** Use `Ash.ActionInput.for_action/4` to specify the resource, the action and its arguments.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'2. **Run the action:** Use `Ash.run_action/2` to execute the action with the prepared input.\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'### Example Usage\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Consider an `Ash.Resource` with the action `:say_hello`:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```elixir\n'[39m +
                    [32m'action :say_hello, :string do\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  argument :name, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  run fn input, _ ->\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    {:ok, "Hello: #{input.arguments.name}"}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'Call this action:\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +

                    [32m'{:ok, greeting} = Resource\n'[39m +
                    [32m'|> Ash.ActionInput.for_action(:say_hello, %{name: "Alice"})\n'[39m +
                    [32m'|> Ash.run_action()\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'IO.puts(greeting)  # Output: Hello: Alice\n'[39m +
                    [32m'```\n'[39m +
                    [32m'\n'[39m +
                    [32m'### Using Code Interface\n'[39m +

                    [32m'action :create_user, :struct do\n'[39m +

                    [32m'  argument :name, :string, allow_nil?: false\n'[39m +

                    [32m'  validate present([:name, :email])\n'[39m +

                    [32m'\n'[39m +

                    [32m'      age: input.arguments.age\n'[39m +
                    [32m'    }}\n'[39m +
                    [32m'  end\n'[39m +
                    [32m'end\n'[39m +
